conditions.name: Floaters & PVD
conditions.description: Posterior vitreous detachment—the gel in your eye shrinks and pulls away, leaving clumps that cast shadows.
key_points: Most floaters are benign and fade with time (your brain learns to ignore them)
No drop or supplement reliably dissolves floaters, but some oral formulations show modest symptomatic benefit
YAG laser works for discrete Weiss rings (single large ring), not diffuse clouds
Sudden shower + flashes + curtain = retinal tear (go to ER immediately)
evidence_based_treatments: Observation / neuroadaptation (60–90% improve subjectively by 6 months)
YAG laser vitreolysis for discrete Weiss ring >6 months post-PVD
Pars plana vitrectomy for severe, refractory cases (cataract risk ~90%)

adjunctive_supplements.name: VitroCap N
adjunctive_supplements.protocol: L-lysine 125 mg, Vit C 40 mg, Vitis vinifera extract 26.3 mg, zinc 5 mg, Citrus aurantium 100 mg
adjunctive_supplements.evidence: Double-blind RCT (n=61, 6 months): P<0.001 reduction in subjective discomfort and objective opacity area; contrast sensitivity P=0.047.

adjunctive_supplements.name: Proteolytic enzyme mix
adjunctive_supplements.protocol: 190 mg bromelain + 95 mg papain + 95 mg ficin per capsule, 1–3 capsules/day
adjunctive_supplements.evidence: Prospective cohort (n=280, 3 months): 65.5–75.5% SVO reduction vs placebo; dose-dependent response.
adjunctive_supplements.commercial_match: Closest option: enteric-coated bromelain 190 mg + papain 95 mg with ficin if available

adjunctive_supplements.name: Curcumin-based supplement (post-YAG)
adjunctive_supplements.evidence: Pilot study (Malandrini et al., 2025): Significant reduction in symptomatic vitreous floaters and foreign-body sensation; improved visual quality.

adjunctive_supplements.name: Low-dose atropine 0.01% drops
adjunctive_supplements.evidence: Small prospective cohort (n=44, ASRS 2025 pilot): 59% satisfaction after 1 week; pupillary dilation may reduce floater salience.

conditions.adjunctive_notes: These are low-risk oral/topical options with early human data. They are investigational, not FDA-approved for floaters, and should be considered adjuncts rather than replacements for observation or procedural treatment.
what_doesnt_work: Castor oil drops (cannot reach vitreous; corneal toxicity risk)
Generic 'floater' supplements without specific formulation data
Eye exercises / Bates method (cannot change axial length)
Collagen or hyaluronic acid supplements for floater reduction
red_flags: Sudden onset of many new floaters (like a shaken snow globe)
Flashes of light in peripheral vision (especially in dark)
Curtain or shadow creeping across vision from any side
Vision loss or distortion (straight lines look wavy)
conditions.when_to_see_doctor: New floaters with flashes? Go today. Sudden shower of floaters + curtain in vision? ER now—retinal detachment can cause permanent vision loss in hours. Routine floaters that are stable for months? Annual dilated exam is fine.

conditions.name: Macular Health (AMD)
conditions.description: Age-related macular degeneration affects the central vision. Early action with the right formula matters.
key_points: AREDS2 formula ONLY helps intermediate AMD (large drusen ≥125µm or pigment changes)
Does NOT prevent AMD in healthy eyes, does NOT treat wet AMD
Smoking = 2–4× risk. Quitting is the single best 'supplement'
Wet AMD needs anti-VEGF injections—no supplement replaces this
evidence_based_treatments: AREDS2 formula: Vit C 500mg, Vit E 400IU, Lutein 10mg, Zeaxanthin 2mg, Zinc 25–80mg, Copper 2mg
Anti-VEGF injections for wet AMD (Eylea, Lucentis, Avastin, Vabysmo)
Lifestyle: Mediterranean diet, leafy greens daily, exercise, BP control, UV protection

amsler_grid.intro: The Amsler grid is an at-home eye test that can help detect early signs of retinal disease such as AMD. If you already have dry AMD, it helps you catch progression to the wet form at an early, treatable stage — when anti-VEGF injections can still dry up the leaking fluid and save vision.
how_to_use: Hold the grid about 12–14 inches away (book-reading distance), with reading glasses on if you wear them.
Cover one eye and stare at the black dot in the center of the grid.
Repeat with the other eye. Test each eye separately — with both eyes open, the good eye can mask changes in the bad one.
Do this once a week. If lines look wavy, dim, irregular, fuzzy, or a section seems blocked out, schedule an eye exam immediately.
amsler_grid.what_changes_mean: An eye without wet AMD usually sees all lines as straight. With wet AMD, fluid accumulates within or under the retina and can form a blister, making straight lines look curved (wavy). Sometimes the fluid interferes with retinal function enough to cause a gray, white, black, or red blind spot in or near the center of the visual field.
amsler_grid.why_it_matters: The fluid comes from new, leaky blood vessels in the retina. It can often be dried up by treatment with anti-VEGF injections (Beovu, Eylea, Lucentis, Avastin) — but only if caught early. Left untreated for months, wet AMD can scar the retina, causing irreversible vision loss. That is why weekly home monitoring matters.
amsler_grid.baseline_note: If your doctor tells you the grid looks fine, check it shortly after your exam to establish your personal baseline. Small areas of waviness can exist from large drusen. The warning sign is a new area, an enlarged area, or a new blind spot — that is when you call the retina specialist.

what_doesnt_work: AREDS2 for early AMD or prevention
Beta-carotene (increases lung cancer in smokers)
Bilberry, saffron, astaxanthin for AMD (insufficient evidence — see our Treatments We're Watching guide)
Stem cell clinics / unproven 'vision restoration' therapies
red_flags: Wavy/distorted straight lines (metamorphopsia)
New central blind spot or blur
Sudden change in color perception
Any sudden vision change in one eye
conditions.when_to_see_doctor: If you're over 50: get a dilated exam every 1–2 years. If you have intermediate AMD: take AREDS2, use Amsler grid weekly, see retina specialist if lines go wavy. Wet AMD? Same-day specialist referral—treatment window is days.

conditions.name: Macular Pucker (ERM)
conditions.description: A thin, scar-like membrane forms on the macula's surface and contracts, wrinkling the retina beneath it. The result: blurred or wavy central vision.
key_points: A translucent membrane grows on the macula's surface and shrinks, 'puckering' the retina — that wrinkling distorts what you see
Usually follows a posterior vitreous detachment: the gel peeling away leaves cells behind that grow into the membrane (70% of ERM patients had a PVD)
Very common — roughly 1 in 11 adults overall, rising steeply with age; most cases are mild or asymptomatic
No drops, supplements, or exercises can remove it — but observation is a legitimate plan for mild cases
Surgery (vitrectomy + membrane peel) is elective, not urgent, and helps most people who need it
evidence_based_treatments: Observation with periodic OCT monitoring — the standard plan for mild or asymptomatic ERM
Pars plana vitrectomy + epiretinal membrane peel for symptomatic distortion or vision loss (typically ≤20/50–20/70); most eyes gain vision, though the macula rarely returns to a perfect contour
Planned cataract surgery coordination — vitrectomy accelerates cataract formation, so many patients combine or sequence the two
what_doesnt_work: Eye exercises or vision therapy — nothing can 'stretch' a contracted membrane
AREDS2 or any supplement — that formula targets AMD, not ERM
Eye drops or injections — there is no medical (non-surgical) therapy for ERM
Amsler-grid practice — the grid monitors change; it does not treat the pucker
red_flags: Sudden worsening of distortion, blur, or vision loss
New flashes or a shower of new floaters (retinal tear risk — especially with a PVD history)
A curtain or shadow across vision
New double vision in one eye
conditions.when_to_see_doctor: Stable, mild pucker? Annual dilated exam with OCT is fine. Distortion or blur that interferes with reading, driving, or daily life? See a retina specialist — surgery is elective and most successful when vision is still relatively good, so don't wait until you can't function. Any red flag above? Call today, not next week.

amsler_grid.intro: The Amsler grid is a useful at-home tool for macular pucker (ERM). The pucker wrinkles the retina, so straight lines can appear wavy or bent — the grid helps you track whether that distortion is stable or worsening between office visits.
how_to_use: Hold the grid about 12–14 inches away (book-reading distance), with reading glasses on if you wear them.
Cover one eye and stare at the black dot in the center of the grid.
Repeat with the other eye. Test each eye separately — with both eyes open, the good eye can mask changes in the bad one.
Do this once a week. If the wavy area grows, a new area appears, or a section seems blocked out, schedule an eye exam.
amsler_grid.what_changes_mean: With macular pucker, the contracting membrane wrinkles the retina, which makes straight lines look wavy or bent — often with mild blur and sometimes objects appearing slightly different sizes between the two eyes. This distortion is usually stable or slowly progressive. A sudden increase in waviness, a new blind spot, or a gray area warrants an exam sooner rather than later.
amsler_grid.why_it_matters: Most puckers are mild and stable, and observation is a legitimate plan. The grid catches change: if distortion is worsening to the point it interferes with reading or driving, that is the conversation to have with a retina specialist about whether surgery (vitrectomy + membrane peel) is right for you. Surgery is elective — but it tends to work best when vision is still relatively good.
amsler_grid.baseline_note: Check the grid shortly after your exam to establish your personal baseline. Some waviness is expected with a pucker — that is the condition. The warning sign is a new area of distortion, an enlarged area, or a new blind spot.
amsler_grid.wavy_caption: the contracting membrane wrinkles the retina, bending straight lines

conditions.name: Dry Eye & Discomfort
conditions.description: Burning, gritty, blurry vision—especially after screens. Usually evaporative dry eye from clogged oil glands (MGD).
key_points: 86% of dry eye is evaporative (MGD)—oil glands clog, tears evaporate too fast
Trifecta: Lipid tears + Omega-3 rTG (2g+) + Warm compresses 2×/day
Prescription drops (Restasis, Xiidra, Tyrvaya) if OTC fails 3 months
Don't put straight castor oil in eyes (corneal toxicity, infection risk)
evidence_based_treatments: Lipid-containing artificial tears (Refresh Mega-3, Systane Complete, Blink Triple Care)
Omega-3 rTG form ≥2g EPA+DHA daily (Nordic Naturals, PRN De3) — takes 6–12 weeks
Warm compresses 10 min 2×/day + lid hygiene (hypochlorous spray)
In-office: IPL, Thermal pulsation (LipiFlow/TearCare), Meibomian gland probing
what_doesnt_work: Straight castor oil in eyes (toxic to cornea, infection risk)
Baby shampoo lid scrubs (destroys lipid layer, use hypochlorous)
Vasoconstrictor drops (Visine, Clear Eyes) — rebound redness
Ethyl ester fish oil (poor absorption)
Blue light glasses for dry eye (weak evidence)
red_flags: Eye pain + light sensitivity + vision change
Severe redness + discharge
Foreign body sensation not improving
Contact lens intolerance developing
conditions.when_to_see_doctor: If OTC tears 4×/day for 3 months don't help: see an optometrist or ophthalmologist. Ask about MGD workup (meibography), prescription drops, or in-office treatments. Dry eye is treatable—you don't have to live with it.

conditions.name: High Eye Pressure (IOP)
conditions.description: Elevated intraocular pressure puts you on the glaucoma-suspect watchlist. Most suspects never develop glaucoma, but IOP is the one risk factor you can influence.
key_points: High IOP is a risk factor, not a diagnosis — most people with ocular hypertension never develop glaucoma
IOP is the ONLY modifiable risk factor for glaucoma; proven treatments (drops, laser) are what actually protect the optic nerve
Caffeine raises IOP acutely, and habitual heavy caffeine raises IOP mainly in people with high genetic risk (UK Biobank, n=121,374)
Supplements are adjuncts at best — none is proven to replace or match prescription IOP treatment
evidence_based_treatments: Monitoring / regular eye exams (visual field + OCT) — the core of glaucoma-suspect care
Prostaglandin analogue eye drops (e.g. latanoprost) — first-line, ~25–33% IOP reduction
Selective laser trabeculoplasty (SLT) — a proven alternative to drops for many patients
Filtering surgery (trabeculectomy / drainage devices) for advanced or refractory cases

adjunctive_supplements.name: Nicotinamide (vitamin B3)
adjunctive_supplements.protocol: 3 g/day in trials — far above the ~16 mg RDA; not self-prescribed, discuss with your doctor first
adjunctive_supplements.evidence: Phase 2 RCT (n=42): oral nicotinamide + pyruvate improved visual field vs placebo (De Moraes, JAMA Ophthalmol 2022). Crossover RCT (n=57): 3 g/day improved inner retinal function on ERG (Hui, Clin Exp Ophthalmol 2020). NOTE: neuroprotection — it does NOT lower IOP. AGS/AAO 2025 position: encouraging but not yet recommended; phase 3 trial (NAMinG) running.
adjunctive_supplements.commercial_match: Generic nicotinamide 500 mg capsules (3 g/day = 6 capsules — again, talk to your doctor)

adjunctive_supplements.name: Mirtogenol (French maritime pine bark + bilberry)
adjunctive_supplements.protocol: 40 mg pine bark + 80 mg bilberry extract, 1–2 tablets/day
adjunctive_supplements.evidence: Small studies show modest IOP reduction (~3 mmHg over 3 months) in ocular hypertension, and it may potentiate latanoprost (Steigerwalt, Mol Vis 2008; Clin Ophthalmol 2010). Small trials, mostly one research group.

adjunctive_supplements.name: Saffron
adjunctive_supplements.evidence: Small RCT in POAG patients on drops: added modest IOP reduction (Jabbarpoor Bonyadi, BMC Complement Altern Med 2014). Single small trial — treat as hypothesis-generating.

adjunctive_supplements.name: Citicoline
adjunctive_supplements.protocol: Oral 500–1000 mg/day, or 0.2% eye drops 3×/day in trials
adjunctive_supplements.evidence: 2023 systematic review/meta-analysis: no significant effect on IOP, visual field, or retinal nerve fiber preservation. Some individual trials show hopeful signals on visual function, but the pooled evidence says no. Skeptical.

conditions.adjunctive_notes: None of these supplements is FDA-approved for high IOP or glaucoma, and none replaces prescribed treatment or regular monitoring. Caffeine reduction is the lifestyle change with the strongest supporting data — especially if you're genetically susceptible. Supplements should be discussed with your ophthalmologist before starting.
what_doesnt_work: Eye exercises / Bates method (cannot change trabecular outflow or IOP)
Mega-dose vitamin C (weak historical data; kidney-stone risk at high doses)
Ginkgo for IOP (blood-flow studies in normal-tension glaucoma, not IOP lowering; bleeding risk)
Omega-3 for IOP (dry-eye evidence does not transfer to IOP)
red_flags: Severe eye pain + nausea/vomiting = possible angle-closure attack (ER now)
Halos around lights + red eye + blurred vision = acute angle closure (ER now)
Sudden vision loss in one eye (ER now)
Rapidly worsening visual field or new blind spots (same-week exam)
conditions.when_to_see_doctor: If you're on a glaucoma-suspect watchlist, keep every scheduled exam — that IS the treatment. IOP fluctuates through the day, so a single normal reading doesn't clear you. New headache + eye pain + nausea? ER now — angle closure can cause irreversible vision loss in hours.
